analysis.one_liner: Repeals federal energy tax credits across all fuel types and lowers the corporate tax rate.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 39 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats, never received a committee vote or any floor action and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have ended more than a dozen federal energy tax breaks at once: credits for ethanol and biodiesel, tax credits for buying electric and fuel-cell vehicles, credits for wind and other renewable electricity, and smaller credits for enhanced oil recovery, marginal wells, advanced nuclear plants, advanced coal and gasification projects, and carbon capture. All of the money saved would have gone to a single, lower flat corporate income tax rate, set by the Treasury Department so the whole package collected the same revenue as before. Individuals would have received no tax cut; the corporate rate cut is the only rate change in the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Corporations and their shareholders, through a lower flat corporate tax rate funded entirely by ending the energy credits. Companies that use few or no energy tax breaks — large profitable retailers, banks, and manufacturers — would have gained the most, since the rate cut applies to all corporations while the repealed credits hit a specific set of energy industries.

how_it_helps.text: It repealed more than a dozen energy tax provisions at once — fuel mixture credits, vehicle purchase credits, production credits for renewables, nuclear, and fossil fuels, and project credits for advanced coal, gasification, and carbon capture.
It directed the full savings to a flat, lower corporate income tax rate, keeping the package revenue-neutral and simplifying the corporate rate structure.

analysis.who_pays: Buyers of electric, plug-in hybrid, and fuel-cell vehicles would have lost purchase credits worth thousands of dollars. Renewable electricity producers, ethanol and biodiesel producers, and developers of nuclear, advanced coal, and carbon capture projects would have lost the credits their projects depend on. Oil and gas producers would have lost the enhanced oil recovery and marginal-well credits, though the lower corporate rate would have partially offset that.
analysis.who_pays_short: EV buyers and subsidized energy producers

drawbacks.text: Buyers of new electric, plug-in hybrid, and fuel-cell vehicles would have lost federal purchase credits, raising the effective price of those vehicles right away, since the plug-in credit repeal took effect on enactment.

The repeal would have stripped federal support from technologies still trying to compete with established energy sources — renewable electricity, advanced nuclear, carbon capture, and advanced coal projects — potentially slowing their deployment.
Every dollar of savings was directed to lowering the corporate tax rate; none went to deficit reduction, individual taxpayers, or direct relief to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The market-level case is real: the bill treated all energy sources the same, cutting subsidies for oil, gas, coal, and nuclear as well as for renewables and biofuels, and it was revenue-neutral by design. But the costs fall on specific, identifiable groups while the benefit is spread thinly across the whole corporate sector. An EV buyer would have lost a purchase credit immediately; capital-intensive clean energy projects that depend on the credits would have lost their main financial support; and households get no direct benefit from the corporate rate cut, whose gains accrue mainly to shareholders. A supporter who wanted deficit reduction or tax relief for individuals gets neither. The bill was never debated or amended, so there is no record of how those design flaws might have been addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 15, 2013 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind.
The bill had 39 cosponsors, all Republicans.
The bill would have repealed energy tax credits spanning fossil fuels, nuclear, and renewables, and directed the savings to a lower flat corporate tax rate set by the Treasury Department.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Recipients of the existing energy tax credits — renewable producers, biofuel blenders, and electric vehicle buyers — kept their credits, and the corporate tax rate was left unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Energy credit recipients; corporate rate unchanged

for.name: Mike Pompeo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 15, 2013 to repeal federal energy tax credits and lower the corporate tax rate; it was referred to Ways and Means the same day.

against.name: Dave Camp
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee (R-MI)
against.what_they_did: The committee took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — for the remainder of the 113th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat is listed as supporting the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have terminated the production credit for electricity from renewable resources and the Section 48 energy credit, the main federal supports for wind, solar, and geothermal projects. These credits have been central to financing renewable buildout.
Repeals the alcohol fuel, biodiesel, and renewable diesel credits and the alternative fuel mixture credit, removing the main federal support for blending biofuels into the fuel supply.

Repeals the plug-in electric drive vehicle credit, the fuel cell motor vehicle credit, and the refueling property credit, raising the effective price buyers pay and removing a sales incentive that helped EVs compete with conventional cars.

Loses the enhanced oil recovery credit and the credit for oil and gas from marginal wells, but every corporation — including oil companies — would have benefited from the lower flat corporate rate, so the net effect depends on how heavily each company relied on the repealed credits.

industries.industry: Nuclear, advanced coal, and carbon capture developers
industries.note: Terminates the credit for production from advanced nuclear power facilities, the advanced coal and gasification project credits, and the carbon dioxide sequestration credit — all supports for capital-intensive projects with long payback periods.

The entire revenue from the subsidy repeal would have funded a lower flat corporate tax rate for all corporations. The gain accrues to profitable corporations and their shareholders, while the offsetting costs fall on EV buyers and on energy industries losing credits.
